report.headline: Hello! It is so great to connect with you. I want to start by acknowledging how incredibly stressful it is to manage a toddler’s meltdown, especially when a sibling is chiming in and adding to the chaos. You were juggling a lot in this moment!

sections.title: You held the boundary
sections.body:
I also want to give you a massive shout-out for something you did exceptionally well: **You held the boundary.** You used a timer (Step 5 of our Screentime Guideline), you gently but firmly removed the phone when time was up, and despite Bryson’s intense crying and begging, *you did not give the phone back* (Step 10). That takes a lot of strength, and it is the absolute foundation of long-term success. You are already doing the hardest part!

As we look at fine-tuning this routine, I want to use a coaching approach to help make these transitions smoother and less exhausting for you.

sections.title: Guided Reflection: The Power of Less Talk
sections.body:
I noticed that while Bryson was crying for the phone, you tried several verbal strategies to get him to stop—explaining why he couldn't have it, telling him he needed to be a "good boy," and eventually using threats like spanking or putting him on YouTube. It is *so* normal to reach for anything we can think of when we are overstimulated by a screaming child!

But I’m curious—**what did you notice about Bryson’s reaction when you explained things or tried to reason with him during the meltdown?**

Take a moment to think about it.

You probably noticed that it didn't slow him down at all; he just kept repeating, "I want your phone!" over and over. When a 4-year-old is in the middle of a tantrum, their "thinking brain" is completely offline. Any extra talking, explaining, or threatening (what we call "nagging" in our guidelines) actually fuels the fire and prolongs the meltdown.

sections.title: Teach & Model: Co-Regulate, then Bridge
sections.body:
Instead of trying to talk Bryson out of his tantrum, we want to shift to a strategy that requires *less* energy from you.

**First: Co-regulate (Step 8)**
When he gets upset, keep your words incredibly brief and neutral. Validate the feeling once, state the boundary, and then stop talking.

**Second: The Bridging Activity (Step 9)**
In the transcript, you told Bryson to "go find your toys or play with your brother." It is very hard for a dysregulated 4-year-old to initiate play on their own. Instead, we want to *draw* him into a new activity.
*Model:* Before you even ask for the phone, set up a highly engaging activity nearby (like blocks, Play-Doh, or a snack). After you take the phone and say your brief co-regulating sentence, sit down at the activity and start playing with it yourself. Narrate what you are doing out loud: *"Wow, I'm putting the red block on the blue block..."*

Do not look at Bryson or try to convince him to join you. Just play. It will feel **very awkward** at first to sit and play with blocks while your child is screaming next to you! I want to normalize that awkwardness—it feels unnatural, but it is incredibly effective. Once he eventually stops crying and comes over to see what you are doing, immediately give him labeled praise: *"I love how you came to play blocks with me!"*

sections.title: Practice & Review
sections.body:
Let's focus on just this one small shift for this week. We aren't going to worry about fixing everything at once. We are just going to replace the extra talking with a "Bridging Activity."

**Your action plan for next time:**
- 1. What is one simple, high-interest activity or toy you can set up on the table *before* the screen time timer goes off?
- 2. When the timer goes off, take the phone, say your one brief sentence ("You're mad, but screen time is over"), and immediately start playing with that toy.

How do you feel about trying this "active ignoring and bridging" technique tomorrow? You are already doing a fantastic job holding the limit; adding this bridge will help Bryson cross over from screen time to playtime much faster!

As we look at fine-tuning this routine, I want to use a coaching approach to help make these transitions smoother and less exhausting for you. 

### 1. Guided Reflection: The Power of Less Talk

### 2. Teach & Model: Co-Regulate, then Bridge

**First: Co-regulate (Step 8)**

### 3. Practice & Review
